title: "Teaching"

I teach research methods and statistics, as instructor of record, as a graduate
teaching assistant across our undergraduate and graduate sequences, and through
an annual R workshop series I run for graduate students.

## Courses

### As instructor of record

::: {.course}
**HDF 315L, Research Methods in Human Development and Family Sciences**\
[The University of Texas at Austin · Fall 2025]{.meta}

Full responsibility for design, instruction, and assessment. Students carried a
single research idea across the semester, with weekly homework building toward
it rather than sitting apart from it.
:::

## Statistics workshops for graduate students

An annual workshop series for graduate students in Human Development and Family
Sciences at UT Austin, run through the departmental statistics committee. Each
runs in January, before the semester gets heavy. Scripts are posted below.

::: {.course}
**AI-assisted data analysis: Vibe coding with Positron** [· January 2026]{.meta}

Working with an AI assistant inside a real analysis project: what it is good
at, where it silently fails, and the verification habits that make it safe to
use on research code.

::: {.entry-links}
[Pilot script](files/workshops/2026/pilot.R)
:::
:::

::: {.course}
**Data wrangling with R** [· January 2025]{.meta}

Reshaping, merging, and cleaning real messy data, which is the unglamorous
majority of any analysis and the part least often taught.
:::

::: {.course}
**Plotting figures with R** [· January 2024]{.meta}

Building publication-quality figures in ggplot2, including the parts that
usually go wrong: legends, facets, fonts, and export settings that survive a
journal's production process.

::: {.entry-links}
[Day 1 script](files/workshops/2024/day1.R)
[Figures lecture](files/workshops/2024/day2-figures.R)
[Exercise](files/workshops/2024/day2-exercise.R)
[Exercise answers](files/workshops/2024/day2-exercise-answers.R)
:::
:::

::: {.course}
**Basic data analysis with R** [· January 2023]{.meta}

A first course for students who had only ever used SPSS: projects, scripts,
reproducibility, and a first pass through descriptives and regression.

::: {.entry-links}
[R basics](files/workshops/2023/00-r-basics.R)
[Analysis with bruceR](files/workshops/2023/01-basic-analysis-bruceR.R)
:::
:::

In development for the coming year: a workshop on the concepts underneath
AI-assisted research, covering tokens, context windows, agents, and the command
line, for researchers with no computing background.

::: {.note}
**Datasets are deliberately not posted.** The workshop examples use participant
data that is not mine to distribute. I am rebuilding the exercises on synthetic
data so the scripts can be run end to end.

**EDIT:** Two files would not copy out of OneDrive because they are stored
online-only: the 2025 data-wrangling `.Rmd` and the 2024 tables lecture `.Rmd`.
Right-click them in Finder, choose "Always Keep on This Device", and tell me;
they will take a few seconds to add. The 2026 and 2024 slide decks are the same
situation.
:::

## AI and computational methods

I am an advanced *user and teacher* of computational methods rather than a
methods developer, and I think that distinction is worth stating plainly. What
I do is bring these tools into applied developmental research and teach other
researchers to use them without losing rigour.

- **Machine learning applied to real data.** Recurrent neural network models of
  student learning trajectories, including feature-importance analyses,
  compared against conventional growth models.
- **Teaching AI-assisted analysis.** I ran our department's January 2026
  workshop, and I am developing the concepts workshop described above.
- **Verification as the discipline that matters.** The point I press hardest in
  teaching: a generated number is a hypothesis until you have re-derived it from
  source output. This is continuous with how I already work.

### What I take from this

This was my first time as instructor of record, and the pattern in the numbers
points at course design rather than delivery. Three things I got wrong, and what
I am changing.

**I did not know the program setting well enough.** HDF 315L is a lower-division
course, so I built it for lower-division students. Almost every student in the
room was a junior or senior, with a single exception. That mismatch explains a
lot: the pacing, the level of scaffolding, and probably the engagement score. I
should have looked at who actually enrols before deciding what to assume.

**Group activities did not work.** I leaned on them because they work well in
the large lecture sections I had been assisting. In a room of nine upper-level
students they produced quiet compliance rather than discussion. Small-group
technique does not scale down; it needs replacing, not shrinking. I am moving
toward structured pair work and written-first protocols where everyone commits
to an answer before anyone speaks.

**I should have talked to students earlier.** I waited for questions and treated
a quiet room as an understanding room. Next time I will use a start-of-semester
survey on background and goals, and short mid-unit check-ins, so I am not
inferring comprehension from silence.

### What the assistantships taught me

The evaluations across four years read differently depending on the room. In the
large child development lectures the recurring theme was responsiveness and
clarity of written feedback. In the graduate statistics sequence it was depth in
R and the detail of feedback on assignments, which is the same strength doing
different work.

Two things to keep working on. One student found my grading somewhat harsh, and
I would rather be exacting *and* visibly on the student's side; those are not in
tension, but I had not made the second part legible. And while several students
described the support as the most useful they had had, one reported getting
little from me across a whole semester. Availability is not outreach. The
students who need help most are the least likely to ask for it, and waiting for
them to arrive is a choice with predictable results.

I have supervised undergraduate research projects in the Perry and Benner labs,
and trained graduate and undergraduate assistants in physiological data
collection and preprocessing: RSA acquisition with Mindware, behavioural coding
with Mangold Interact, and the cleaning pipelines that come after.
